title: Making Oil Companies Pay for Climate Damages
text:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts 

 A wildfire is called that for a reason. It can be unpredictable, possibly unmanageable, and then tragic and expensive. For a long time, cities and counties dealing with increasing occurrences of wildfires, hurricanes, heat domes, and other extreme weather events treated them as costs they simply had to bear in an era of climate change. After all, what else can they do when there’s no one to blame for a disaster?

 About 20 years ago, a group of scientists started to think differently about these events. They began to turn the very general cause-and-effect science of climate change into something much more specific. This emerging discipline asked the question: What if you could scientifically attribute individual extreme events to climate change? That idea led to an even more practical question: What if you could use what amounts to forensic accounting to sue oil companies to pay for the damage caused by carbon emissions?

 This was a rare development to break through what activists have started to refer to as “climate despair.” Dozens of cities, counties, and states have begun suing energy giants using this new discipline of climate-attribution science. Now the Supreme Court will decide whether these cases can move forward. The justices opened the fall term last month with oral arguments in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County . Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself because of his investments in oil companies, so for their suit to proceed, the Boulder litigants need only one conservative justice to flip. 

 In the oral arguments, Chief Justice John Roberts raised a prospect that should terrify the oil companies, and their shareholders: If the litigants were to prevail, he speculated, “a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit.”

 The Atlantic staff writer Ross Andersen, who wrote about the science of climate attribution , joins Radio Atlantic to discuss the Supreme Court case, the strange questions it raises, and the potential brave new world in which communities could simply sue fossil-fuel companies for the impacts of climate change.  

 The following is a transcript of the episode: 

 Hanna Rosin: If you can think of a big-name climate-protection policy, it’s likely that President Trump has made moves to roll it back.

 President Trump: It’s the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world, in my opinion, climate change. No matter what happens, you’re involved in that.

 Rosin: The Paris Agreement, the UN climate framework, Obama’s clean-power rule, California’s emission rules, EV subsidies, et cetera.

 Trump: All of these predictions made by the United Nations and many others, often for bad reasons, were wrong. They were made by stupid people that have cost their countries fortunes and given those same countries no chance for success. If you don’t get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail.

 Rosin: This week, world leaders are in Turkey for COP, the annual United Nations climate-change conference. America didn’t send an official delegation, the second year in a row the federal government entirely skipped it. For people who care about how human actions can harm the environment, the reversal of progress has led to what people are calling “climate despair,” or as staff writer Ross Andersen puts it, “climate nihilism.”

 Ross Andersen: When I think back 10 years, right? Or a little more than 10 years to, like, the late Obama era, at that time, there were all these reasons for optimism.

 You know, the Paris Agreement, like, the ink was fresh on that. The Clean Power Plan had been somewhat of a success, regulating carbon emissions in the United States. And it seemed like acceptance of climate change being real was sort of under way.

 And then the last 10 years, I think, it’s just been a different story. Some 60 percent of Americans now say that they really don’t expect not just our government but humanity as a whole to get its act together in time to solve this problem.

 And look, it’s never been a winner. You and I both know it’s hard to get audiences excited about—

 Rosin: Yeah.

 Andersen: —thanks for listening, everyone. ( Laughs .)

 Rosin: ( Laughs .)

 Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . While many people have gotten stuck in their despairing, nihilistic ways, a group of climate researchers have spent decades developing what Ross calls “An Existential Threat to the Oil Industry.” That’s the headline of his article about the evolving science of what’s called “climate attribution.”

 Now what has been percolating through academia has reached courtrooms across the country. Cities, counties, and states have filed dozens of lawsuits—including one that went before the Supreme Court for its first argument of the term.

 The science is complex, but there’s a simple idea at its core: If fossil fuels cause pollution, and that pollution incurs costs on cities and states, why can’t the people that live in those cities and states just sue the fossil-fuel companies?

 Rosin: Ross, welcome to the show.

 Andersen: Hanna, thanks for having me.

 Rosin: So Ross, what is “climate attribution”?

 Andersen: Yeah, climate-attribution science. So this is the science that—we know the climate is changing already. We know the Earth is getting warmer, and scientists are taking a look at that and saying, Whose fault is this? You know? Who is responsible for the Earth getting warmer? 

 And it started as just attributing the phenomena of climate change to humans. So, people had wondered, like, Well, what about some of the individual events? If there’s a really bad hurricane, if there’s a really bad wildfire or a drought, can we say that that particular event was caused by humans? 

 And at first, the answer was: Absolutely not. The atmosphere is super dynamic. Saying that this particular event, that we can just definitively attribute that to humans, was just a bridge too far, scientifically.

 But then, in the early 2000s, there was an atmospheric scientist named Myles Allen in the U.K., and he wrote a very famous editorial for Nature , in which he made the case that, Hey, we ought to try to do this. And this was not just a purely unmotivated inquiry in search of truth. He was saying specifically, Let’s do this because this could be useful in lawsuits .

 He looked at the success that some of the epidemiologists had with cancer and tobacco. The proper question in his view was not Can we tie these particular cigarettes to this particular person’s lung cancer? It was, Look, how much more likely did smoking make that person getting cancer? 

 Rosin: Right. Okay, before we get to how it was used in the world, I just wanna understand the science, its limitations. Can you talk me through that a little bit? What is the science, how did it evolve, and what are its limitations?

 Andersen: Okay. Let’s do a really simple attribution. Let’s take a heat wave, a really extreme one. Let’s imagine that in October, we were to have a stretch of 110-degree days here in Washington, D.C. And we wanna know, should we be attributing this to humans? This seems crazy.

 The right scientific question there is: How much more likely is that kind of event, that heat wave, in a world with emissions versus a world without? Now, if we wanna compare those two things, we do have some records about what a world without emissions was like, right? We have a historical record that goes back, at least in the United States, more than 100 years. Not much more, but more than 100 years.

 Weather caster 1: Good morning, and welcome to October, a month that often produces some of our finest days of the year.

 Andersen: But that’s not enough, right? Because the atmosphere is so dynamic, the Earth may behave in many, many, many different ways with the exact amount of carbon in the atmosphere every year.

 Weather caster 2: Gonna be another nice day. I mean, I’m just gonna be on repeat every day this week. It’s gonna be chilly in the mornings.

 Rosin: Right. Like, there are just too many variables to say for certain: Emissions is the difference, is the main difference.

 Andersen: Correct. Instead of 100 Octobers, we need 1,000 Octobers. But we don’t have records for the year 1026, do we? And so what we have to do is generate 1,000 Octobers in a computer.

 Weather caster 1: Good morning, and welcome to October.

 Weather caster 2: Gonna be another nice day. I mean, I’m just gonna be on repeat every day this week.

 [ Echoes ] 

 Andersen: And what we’re doing with those thousand Octobers is: We’re getting 1,000 Octobers in our emissions world, and then we’re getting 1,000 Octobers without emissions. And we’re looking for that one-week heat wave in each of them, how many times it shows up, and then we’re comparing those and that’s how we decide, Oh, it was this much more likely in a world with emissions. 

 Rosin: That’s interesting. But if we don’t know all the variables, how do we know all the variables? Like, how do you input the variables if you’re not sure what the variables are?

 Andersen: Well, Hanna, you’re very smart, so you’ve come immediately to the crux of the problem here.

 Rosin: Yeah. ( Laughs .)

 Andersen: Yeah, all this stuff lives in a computer, and I wanna say, Look, our climate models are good and getting better and have been getting better, so it’s not like these guys are throwing darts at a dartboard here .

 The science has really, really advanced, and there’s tons of data about how the atmosphere works, and climate and weather and all the rest. But yes, we are generating simulations of weather in order to do this science.

 Rosin: Right, so predicting all the variables is one issue. I’m sure there are others.

 Andersen: Yeah, for sure. I mean, first of all, this science doesn’t work equally well for every kind of extreme weather event. We wish that we had a magical science that would tell us whether hurricanes, wildfires, droughts, and all the rest were caused by human climate change, but it’s not that simple. So heat waves, because what you’re measuring is heat and the climate has gotten hotter, it’s kind of like a direct causal line.

 But there are other kinds of events, like wildfires, where you have all kinds of confounding factors, like ignition and how a forest has been managed, et cetera, et cetera. Those are much more difficult to attribute. But it’s not definitive, right? This is like a probabilistic analysis. It’s different to say that something was made more likely versus it was caused.

 Rosin: I just want to be clear about one thing. The attribution science is attributing these events to human behavior generally, to a specific human behavior, to a company. Who is the science pointing a finger at as responsible?

 Andersen: That’s a great question because the kinds of attribution that I’ve been describing so far are only pointing the finger at all of us, at human carbon emissions.

 But you can pair them with another bit of science, or really kind of forensic accounting, that’s been done principally by a guy named Richard Heede.

 Richard Heede: In order to address this issue, we needed to look at the corporations themselves and what kind of assets they had that imperiled the future of climate change.

 Andersen: He’s a scientist in Colorado who has been really scouring the planet for business records from oil companies going back to the 19th century.

 Rosin: Oh, interesting.

 Andersen: And because they have to report these things, he’s been able to assemble this massive database that is—it’s been peer reviewed. It’s never been really substantively contested, but basically gives us kind of an apportionment for big oil companies. He’s able to say that ExxonMobil, which was Standard Oil previously, is responsible for something like 3 percent of human carbon emissions, and give a number like that for something like 100 different companies.

 Heede: I’ve just ranked the top 12 investor-owned and state-owned corporations here, in terms of their percentage of global industrial emissions since 1750 through 2015.

 Andersen: And so to tie a bow on it, if you and I were looking to sue because we are so outraged about this imaginary October heat wave that had struck Washington, D.C., made our lives miserable, caused infrastructure damage, whatever else, we can go to that initial bit of attribution science that tells us that heat wave was made 10 times more likely by human carbon emissions.

 And then we can say, Okay, but we’re not suing all of humanity. We want, like, people with some deep pockets. And we can batch together the Exxons and the Chevrons of the world, who maybe chip in 3 percent each, and get up to something like 50 percent and say, We wanna sue them .

 There are now dozens of cities and counties and states and all the rest who have really seized on this research, and filed lawsuits against the oil giants. Not just one, but as I was saying, 10 or 15 oil companies. And each of those cases is at various stages, right? And none of them has yet gone to trial, crucially.

 Rosin: So this being a relatively new science, I imagine there are questions about it that come up once it becomes evidence in a legal case. It goes under a different level of scrutiny. Is that what happened?

 Andersen: Yeah, that’s exactly right. If and when these cases go to trial, judges are going to—first of all, before a jury even sees it, they have to decide whether this evidence is admissible at all. And different courts in different states use different standards, but really, they’re looking for what you might expect. Like: Is this reproducible? Does it have the respect of mainstream scientists? 

 And, look, the energy companies are gonna fight hard against it. But I think on admissibility, this is just—now I’m speculating free rein here, but my sense is there’s a good argument for this being admissible. This has been absorbed by top institutions in the sciences. This is not a fringe science. But admissible doesn’t mean it’s convincing in front of the jury.

 Rosin: Hearing you talk about it, I realize if it turns out to be admissible and they do go to trial, it is a pretty interesting conceptual shift. For one thing, it takes something like climate change, which is abstract, you know?

 Like, when I think of “hurricane,” my mind naturally thinks of: multifactorial. Like, it comes from a lot of different places, and it kind of reduces it to very concrete harms. There’s a cause; there’s an effect. There’s a person who’s responsible; there are victims. Like, it does make the whole situation a lot more digestible.

 Andersen: I think that’s right. And I think against that, opposing counsel, right, is gonna say that, actually, you know, our previous human culture and insurance policies that regarded these things as acts of God probably had the right idea—that actually, the science isn’t quite there and, you know, remains sort of probabilistic.

 And, you know, there’s gonna be an interesting conversation around the motivation of some of these scientists. Because right or wrong—I tend to think right—a lot of these scientists have involved themselves in climate activism, as you might expect if you were one of the world’s experts responsible for looking at this data, and had come to the conclusion that, you know, the entire planet and all of its ecosystems were endangered by it.

 Rosin: Hmm. In some ways, this scenario that you’re describing and that the scientists are looking at has, like, a very straightforward, populist appeal. Like, We suffered. Make the oil companies pay for it , which in this social-political climate does have resonance.

 Andersen: Yeah, it does. And I think especially during the Trump administration, when it seems like all guardrails have come off the big corporations, like, I think about this as an analogy to the data-center debate.

 Rosin: Yeah, yeah.

 Andersen: Right? With the big tech companies, where I’m not always sold, you know, on the, like, extreme ecological impacts of the data centers, like, I think there’s probably actually a way to do it in a way that actually doesn’t have an extreme ecological impact. And yet, I think people are hungry, and I understand this hunger that they have to have some kind of pressure point of leverage against these companies.

 One of the most fascinating conversations I had was with Jonathan Adler, who’s a law professor at William & Mary, and who one of his colleagues described him to me as America’s only conservative environmental-law professor.

 Rosin: ( Laughs .) Mm-hmm.

 Andersen: And what he said—and he was sort of offering me the landscape of all the different ways that this science would be contested in court—but what he said was: The oil companies, they don’t wanna get to that stage .

 Because, look, these are not sympathetic defendants. No matter what your politics are, an oil company is this kind of massive corporate behemoth that is emitting stuff into the sky, or helping emit stuff into the sky, and has lots of money and all these things.

 And so I just feel like he was saying that: You get them in a room with a jury—who knows what can happen.

 [ Break ] 

 Rosin: So, Ross, climate-attribution science is now at the Supreme Court.

 Chief Justice John Roberts: We’ll hear argument, first this term, in Case 25-170, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County .

 Rosin: What is this Boulder, Colorado, case about?

 Andersen: Yes. The city and county of Boulder, Colorado, are suing Suncor and ExxonMobil for damages from climate change, you know, like wildfires, which have increased greatly, and they’re expecting to increase even more in the future.

 Rosin: Mm-hmm. And oral arguments happened in October. What were the main questions that the Court considered?

 Andersen: The Court is not looking at the attribution science itself. What they’re doing is ruling on a preemption issue, and this actually goes back to the aughts because these are not the first climate cases.

 There actually were a run of them in the early and mid-2000s. But they filed them as federal claims. And they were thrown out of court. First, you know, they said: This is a political question. This is Congress’s job to regulate fossil fuels, not the job of the courts .

 And then in a later decision, the Supreme Court itself said: Look, none of these cases can go through. They’re actually preempted by the Clean Air Act .

 Rosin: What is preemption?

 Andersen: Preemption is the Court saying that it’s the right and job of the federal government to regulate emissions that come from not just all over the country, but all over the world—and furthermore, the federal government is doing that job with this specific legislation called the Clean Air Act.

 Rosin: So the question before the Court is: Does Boulder, Colorado, even have the right to bring this in court?

 Andersen: Yes, that’s exactly right. Because in the 2000s, these plaintiffs tried to bring these claims in federal court. They got tossed out. They said, Hey, we’ve got federal law for this already .

 Rosin: Like, the Clean Air Act takes care of this.

 Andersen: Yes. Correct.

 Rosin: Got it. Okay.

 Andersen: And so now they’re trying to bring them in the state court, and the Colorado Supreme Court said, Great. Happy to have it in state court . And so then the oil companies appealed to the Supreme Court and said, They can’t do this in state court either .

 Now, if Boulder loses before the Supreme Court, then all of these cases go away because we already know they can’t be filed in federal court, and this would essentially shut the door to state claims.

 Andersen: What’s interesting about this idea that kind of governs this, the whole case for the oil companies, is this notion that fossil-fuel emissions ought to be regulated by the Clean Air Act.

 The Trump administration, they’ve kind of, like, decided not to do it at all. Like, they famously at the beginning of this administration have rescinded the endangerment finding, the notion that we are endangered by carbon emissions at all, and have really done everything in their power not to regulate CO2.

 So they have a weird job in court saying, The Clean Air Act is supposed to do this , when, you know, they’re actually not using the Clean Air Act.

 And actually, Justice Gorsuch, of all people, really keyed in on this.

 Justice Neil Gorsuch:  As I understand it, EPA has disclaimed the power to regulate greenhouse gases, not just from motor vehicles, but more recently from stationary sources too. So this—does the Clean Air Act change anything?

 Rosin: You know, it’s especially interesting to hear this line of questioning from Gorsuch, because Justice Samuel Alito, conservative justice, recused himself from this case because of his investments in oil companies.

 Andersen:  Yeah, and it’s interesting. I mean, that sort of skews how we handicap this. Because now you have the three liberal justices that seem to be sympathetic to Boulder. And then you only need one of the conservative justices because Colorado’s Supreme Court ruled in favor of Boulder. So if they’re deadlocked at 4–4, that means that the Colorado Supreme Court’s ruling stands, at least for now.

 Rosin: Mm-hmm. So it is actually a live issue. Now, Justice Elena Kagan raised a comparison in the oral arguments that’s often made with these kinds of cases, which is lawsuits against tobacco companies.

 Justice Elena Kagan: This suit appears to be based on the old 1990s tobacco suits that were brought by states and local governments, basically saying that Big Tobacco had made representations, misrepresentations, which had caused people to overuse the product, causing harm to those governments.

 I suppose the opioid litigation more recently follows the same model. This is chapter three.

 Rosin: What do you make of that comparison?

 Andersen: Yeah. I think there are several fascinating parallels. To me, the most interesting one is that, you know, when the tobacco companies were sued, the discovery process shook loose these documents that showed that, actually, for years and years they had said, Hey, people are making a free choice to smoke. We’re not twisting anybody’s arm. 

 Nightline : After all, they have warned us. And each of us is a free agent who can choose to smoke, or not smoke.

 Andersen: And, after these cases, you know, after you had discovery in these cases, it showed that they, all that time, had known that their products were causing cancer. And so there was an argument to be made that actually, people did not have a free choice, because the tobacco companies had deliberately manipulated the information environment around their product.

 Nightline : But what if someone could prove that beginning in 1953, the tobacco industry developed a joint strategy to deny the dangers, pretend to be doing relevant research, and prevent regulation? Would that make the industry liable?

 Andersen: And so a lot of people think, and there’s already been lots of public evidence that the oil companies know that burning oil heats up the Earth. And so if you have documents, you know, further documents come out over the course of discovery in these cases, that could make, you know, the oil companies—could put them in a tough position.

 Rosin: I see. That seems important. That seems important. One of the phrases that got repeated a lot during oral arguments was that Suncor and Exxon, the two oil companies, are producers, not emitters.

 Kannon Shanmugam: Remember that my clients are not emitters. My clients are producers of fossil fuels.

 Rosin: What does that mean?

 Andersen: I wouldn’t wanna mistake that for just a legal technicality, because I think it gets to just a fascinating heart of this whole issue. In suing oil companies, as all of these suits do—you know, they have as their defendants the big oil giants, and there’s something satisfying about that, right?

 Because they’re really rich, you know, and they can pay out these settlements and, you know, as I said before, they’re not terribly sympathetic defendants. But they aren’t actually the ones burning the oil, right? We’re burning the oil.

 Rosin: I see. Like, why aren’t you suing me for filling my car up at the Exxon station?

 Andersen: —Yeah. Why is Hanna Rosin not a named defendant in Suncor ? That’s what I came here to ask. ( Laughs .)

 Rosin: No, it’s a totally reasonable. That’s an interesting philosophical question. Yeah. You know? And maybe it’s related to the tobacco question in the sense, like: Have we created an infrastructure with alternatives the way, say, they have in Europe? Have we created government incentives—

 Andersen: Mm-hmm.

 Rosin: —for me not to fill my car up with Exxon? Do I have another choice?

 Andersen: Yeah. Well, for me, it weakens the deception argument, right? Because, you know, we’ve had a lot of time now where a lot of us—not all of us, you know (some people don’t subscribe to climate science), but a lot of us—have had good reason to believe that carbon emissions are causing climate change, and yet we haven’t meaningfully changed our behavior, right?

 I haven’t. I drive a car. I get on airplanes, and do all kinds of things. You know, I have plastic in my house, whatever. And I think if you’re going to hold these companies, the producers, liable for these enormous sums of money, yeah, it’s gonna be difficult.

 Rosin: Mm-hmm. Now, on the other side of the balance sheet, Chief Justice Roberts laid out what seemed like a pretty scary outcome for oil companies if Boulder wins.

 Roberts: Presumably, if you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit, probably copy your pleadings, and then there’ll be at least 50 causes of action filed. How would you think that will work out on the ground?

 Rosin: So what do you think about that scenario? How realistic is it?

 Andersen: You know, when I asked, when I was working on this story, I asked law professors about this, and one thing that I heard again and again was that the courts are totally fine with big judgments and verdicts.

 Like, they’re happy to bankrupt a company, even a big oil company.

 Rosin: ( Laughs. )

 Andersen: They’re down.

 Rosin: Interesting.

 Andersen: What they don’t like is uncertain or infinite liability.

 Rosin: Oh, okay.

 Andersen: And so the thing that I heard there is that if they could successfully argue that this kind of thing would lead to infinite liability.

 Rosin: Now, what is that line? That line is that it has to be pretty clear. Like, it can’t apply to every scenario? It has to be a certain amount of damage or a certain specificity of attribution?

 Andersen: Yeah. I don’t know what the threshold is or will be. But I think that, you know, if you have the view of climate change that I do, Roberts is right that virtually every municipality would have some claim to be affected by it.

 Rosin: What about the idea that the oil companies argued that this is ultimately a political question? Like, not a question for the courts. Congress has to decide how they wanna regulate.

 Andersen: Yeah. I’m sympathetic to that argument. Not wholly. I’m not saying, you know, I’m on their side. But I would hope that this wouldn’t be the final accounting. Like I said earlier when we were talking about the data-center comparison, maybe this is just useful as a kind of leverage point until we get not a final settlement, because there are no such things in politics, but we get a law that feels a little bit more settled, you know.

 And look, I think just by the nature of the problem, it’s gonna be—it has to be global, right? 

 Whatever generation gets to a genuine resolution on this issue, where climate change is both halted and people feel that they’ve been made whole for whatever damage that it’s caused, it just strikes me that it’s not gonna be through litigation, that there’s gonna have to be some new law or resolution.

 Rosin: I see. So this is both pessimistic and optimistic. What you’re saying is even if the states and counties lose in Court, if Boulder loses in Court, there’s still left a kind of pressure.

 I mean, we started this episode talking about climate despair, climate nihilism. It feels like where we’re ending is: The genie is out of the bottle. Like, this idea is out there. It’s being taken seriously, both by scientists and by courts in some realm, and it’s not gonna go away.

 Andersen: I don’t think so. I think the science is gonna move on. You know, I expect attribution science to be better in 10 years. If it’s not this batch of claims, I think there’ll be another batch of claims, you know, in the fullness of time. We’ll see.

 Rosin: Ross, thank you so much for joining me today.

 Andersen: Hanna, thanks for having me on.

 Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Jacob Smollen. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Fact-checking by Hana Kiros and Sam Fentress. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

 If you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener .

 I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.
